<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but PRO stayed closer to the motion as written and controlled the decisive frame: the disclosure default operates upstream of the clinic door, so every harm CON catalogued (unmonitored medication, uncontested claims, the hallway at 3am) presupposes a patient who arrived. PRO's flip on the dependency structure ([A2.2]) — CON cannot invoke family-plan dependency to demand "pay your own way" — was clean, as was "suspicion carries strictly less information than the EOB" ([A4.2]), which blunted CON's best pressure question. CON's strongest move was the available-vs-default distinction ([B4.2]) plus the two-populations weighing (deterred mild self-referrers vs. severe cases who arrive through others), and CON correctly caught PRO's overreading of [B4.3] in the closing. But CON's fallback — confidentiality on request at intake, backed by clinician judgment — largely concedes the resolution as written, which targets billing that *automatically* reveals the visit; PRO's "a right you must invoke inside a system you already fear is designed to fail the fearful" ([A5.4]) exploited that better than CON's "easiest sentence in the room" rebuttal repaired it. CON did win the unresolved sub-issue of appeals, miscoding, and collections, which PRO answered thinly, but CON never showed that administrative standing outweighs treatment initiation. CON also took a small execution cost for a clipped rebuttal. Both sides used the A1:/A2: format properly and asked genuinely pointed questions.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question — a "targeted exception with clinician judgment" requires a clinician, which requires the patient to walk in, which the disclosure default forecloses — forced CON into the opt-in-at-intake fallback ([B4.1]). That answer was honest and well-put, but it moved CON's position close to affirming the motion, and PRO's "defaults decide behavior; the envelope is the door" ([A5.4]) capitalized on it.</best_rebuttal>
